questions.prompt_en: Some people believe that governments should fine people who repeatedly fail to separate recyclable waste. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
questions.prompt_vi: State a consistent position; evaluate conditions under which fines are justified.

answer.model_en:
Some people argue that governments should impose fines on residents who repeatedly fail to separate recyclable waste. I partly agree with this suggestion because penalties may improve behaviour, but they should only be introduced when recycling services are convenient and clear.

There are good reasons to use fines in some situations. When recycling rules are easy to understand, a small number of people may still ignore them because they consider separating waste inconvenient. A warning followed by a reasonable fine could encourage these residents to take the rules more seriously. In addition, better separation makes it easier for local authorities to process materials such as paper, glass and metal. As a result, less usable material may be sent to landfill. It may also become easier for recycling workers to sort what is collected, since different materials are less likely to be mixed together.

However, punishment alone would be unfair if households do not have suitable facilities. For example, residents of an apartment building might not have separate bins or enough information about collection times. In such cases, a fine would not solve the underlying problem. Governments should therefore provide accessible recycling points and simple instructions before introducing penalties. Schools and community groups could also explain why separating waste matters.

In conclusion, I agree that repeated refusal to recycle can justify a fine, but only after authorities have provided practical support and clear warnings. An approach combining education, convenient facilities and proportionate penalties is more likely to be effective than punishment on its own.
